questions.q: What is Kafka's core data structure, according to this lesson?
options: A durable, ordered log — events stay for a configured retention period, not removed once read
A traditional message queue where each message disappears once a worker consumes it
A relational database table
An in-memory cache with no persistence
questions.explain: Unlike a traditional queue, Kafka retains every event for a configured period, readable by many independent consumers.

questions.q: Why can two different consumers read the same Kafka topic at completely different points without affecting each other?
options: Because reading a message doesn't remove it from the log — each consumer tracks its own position independently
Kafka only allows one consumer to read a topic at a time
Consumers must always start reading from the very beginning
Kafka deletes a message as soon as any consumer reads it
questions.explain: One consumer can read from offset 0 while another reads from offset 500, entirely independently, since nothing is removed.

questions.q: How does Kafka's replay property make Kappa architecture (Career & Capstone Lesson 7) actually work in practice?
options: Reprocessing history means replaying the same log through the same consumer logic, not standing up a separate batch job
Kafka has nothing to do with Kappa architecture
Kappa architecture requires deleting all historical events immediately
Replay only works for the very first message ever written
questions.explain: This is exactly the property Career & Capstone Lesson 7 depended on — a durably replayable source.

questions.q: How does Kafka relate to what was already taught in Fabric & Real-Time Analytics's Eventstreams, per this lesson?
options: Kafka is the vendor-neutral version of the same real-time ingestion idea Eventstreams solves inside the Fabric ecosystem
Kafka and Eventstreams solve completely unrelated problems
Eventstreams are built directly on top of Kafka with no differences at all
Kafka replaces the need to ever learn Eventstreams
questions.explain: Chapter 4's Lesson 20 makes this comparison explicit, concept by concept, once Kafka's own vocabulary is established.
